teaches: A surprising off-beat move is not the same as a mistake, but it rarely reflects deep preparation — meet it with calm, textbook play rather than trying to punish it at once. The refutation of a sideline is usually just sound development.
explains: The pawn to c4 grabs a bit of space — but it hands over the d4 square for good, because White no longer has a c-pawn to ever support that break. Don't reach for fireworks to punish it; this is a sideline you answer with simple, sound positional chess.

line: e4 c5 c4 Nc6 Nc3 g6 d3 Bg7
teaches: A fianchetto that rakes the long diagonal is a logical developing move whatever the specific opening — especially when it aims straight at a square the opponent has weakened. Point your best piece at the hole.
explains: The bishop develops to g7 and rakes down the long diagonal, aimed right at the d4 square that White's early c-pawn push left soft for good. Nothing clever, just the natural move — the best piece pointed at the weakness.

line: e4 c5 c4 Nc6 Nc3 g6 d3 Bg7 Nf3 d6
teaches: Order your developing moves to keep your best piece's diagonal open — delay the natural knight development that would block your own fianchettoed bishop, and play the useful pawn move first.
explains: Pawn to d6 comes first. The natural knight to f6 would wall in the g7-bishop and loosen the grip on d4 — so we hold it back and route that knight to e7 instead. The pawn move is useful anyway and prepares a later central break.

line: e4 c5 c4 Nc6 Nc3 g6 d3 Bg7 Nf3 d6 Be2 Bg4
teaches: There is more than one way to remove a key enemy defender — besides the usual pawn levers, simply pinning and trading it off with a bishop is an option players often overlook, and it is exactly the piece guarding the squares you want.
explains: The bishop comes to g4, pinning the knight on f3 and preparing to trade it off. That knight guards the central d4 and e5 squares — the whole fight in this structure — so removing it is worth the bishop.

line: e4 c5 c4 Nc6 Nc3 g6 d3 Bg7 Nf3 d6 Be2 Bg4 O-O Bxf3
teaches: General rules bow to a concrete priority — in a closed centre, giving up the bishop pair to remove a defender of the key squares is worth more than the abstract advantage of the two bishops. The position, not the maxim, decides.
explains: Yes, taking the knight hands over the bishop pair — the rule says keep it. But the rule bows to the position here: the centre is closed, so the two bishops matter little, and this trade removes a defender of the squares Black is fighting for. Development is untouched.
